caveats: ATO denotes average treated outcome, ATT average treatment gain among treated units, and TT total treatment gain; the average rewards are defined to be zero when no unit is treated.

The general average-reward formula uses countable covariates, i.i.d. evaluation observations and independent treatment draws conditional on covariates; its ATT branch additionally conditions estimator unbiasedness on the full covariate and treatment vectors.

Fixed-query unbiasedness does not suffice for a sample-dependent estimator evaluated on its own data; the corrected alignment and information results impose the relevant conditional treated-residual moment and integrability assumptions.

The corrected ranking theorem requires a common untreated conditional mean, integrable reference effects and each individual weighted reward summand to be integrable; finiteness of only the total score is insufficient.

Ranking optimality uses all measurable treatment-probability policies taking values in $[0,1]$; the information bound permits a feasible subclass but assumes supplied score and welfare maximizers rather than proving their existence.
The general uniform-error regret inequality is an abstract optimization lemma; connecting a particular counterfactual score to its hypothesis requires the separate probabilistic assumptions.
The finite witnesses and general population theorems do not by themselves verify the empirical Horse Colic or Stroke Trial analyses.

corrections.what: The printed ATO and ATT rule treating only covariate values with the largest positive mean need not maximize finite-sample reward: in a two-unit example with zero baseline and effects $(9/10,1)$, the printed rule $(0,1)$ earns $3/4$, while the unique reward maximizer $(17/18,1)$ earns $1369/1440$ and has welfare regret $1/40$.

In place of the printed conditional-average objective and associated best-response rule, the corrected i.i.d. discrete-covariate statement gives unconditional zero-on-empty reward $[1-(1-q)^n]A/q$ for $q=E[\pi(X)]>0$ and zero for $q=0$, with best responses maximizing this objective, where $A=E[\mu_1(X)\pi(X)]$ for ATO or $A=E[\tau(X)\pi(X)]$ for ATT under its additional full-vector conditional unbiasedness and integrability assumptions.

Against the use of fixed-covariate unbiasedness to justify incentive alignment, two one-unit experiments have baseline estimates unbiased at each fixed covariate but biased at the evaluation covariate, causing reward-maximizing and welfare-maximizing policies to disagree with welfare regret $1/2$.

Replacing the insufficient fixed-covariate unbiasedness premise by conditional mean zero of the treated baseline-estimation residual and its integrability, the corrected TT theorem makes expected reward equal sample size times mean welfare, equates reward and welfare maximizers on every admissible feasible class, and gives each attained best response zero regret.

The printed absolute-continuity direction in Theorem 2 does not ensure the displayed reference density exists: uniform probability on $[0,1]$ is absolutely continuous with respect to its half-uniform, half-point-mass reference law with the same support, while the reverse direction and a density representing that reference law fail.

Replacing Theorem 2's reversed absolute continuity and inadequate unbiasedness premises by reference-law absolute continuity with respect to each agent law, treated-evaluation conditional unbiasedness and integrability of each weighted reward term, the corrected theorem identifies optimal scores as reference means of positive effects and proves uniform rank preservation, with relative rank preservation when effects are nonnegative.

key_results.what: For every positive regret threshold, a two-unit binary-covariate experiment has an actual best response to the average-treated-outcome reward whose welfare regret exceeds that threshold.

Two agents with identical constant treatment effect one, common covariate laws and a perfect zero baseline have optimal unnormalized total-treatment-gain scores one and two at sample sizes one and two, violating both ranking desiderata for the ordered pair.
If a score differs from welfare by at most $\gamma$ uniformly on a feasible policy set, and score and welfare maxima are attained, every supplied score maximizer has welfare regret at most $2\gamma$.

Under the corrected conditional unbiasedness assumption at treated observations given public and private covariates, the stated integrability conditions and supplied score and welfare maximizers, total-treatment-gain best-response regret is at most $2\gamma$ whenever $\gamma$ bounds the mean absolute difference between the full-information and public-covariate untreated means.

overview.overview: This work studies how rewards based on counterfactual outcomes affect treatment-policy incentives, comparisons between agents and welfare regret under private information. The Lean development covers finite reward counterexamples, arbitrarily large regret for average treated outcomes, and corrected expected-reward, alignment, ranking and information-bound statements. Its repairs distinguish unbiasedness at a fixed covariate from unbiasedness at treated evaluation observations and retain the probability of treating nobody in finite-sample average rewards.

text.body: The Lean statements formalize the counterexample with two units of P006-E001. There are two equally likely types $x\in\{0,1\}$, with $Y(0)=0$, $\hat\mu_0=0$, and $Y(1)$ equal to $9/10$ for type $0$ and to $1$ for type $1$. A policy is a pair $(u,v)=(\pi(0),\pi(1))$ in the unit square. The expected reward is the exact sum over the 16 combinations of types and treatments, and the reward is $0$ when nobody is treated. The main statement asserts that the printed rule is $(0,1)$ and has expected reward $3/4$, while the policy that treats everyone has expected reward $19/20$. It asserts further that every policy has expected reward at most $1369/1440$, with equality only at $(17/18,1)$. The policy that treats everyone maximizes welfare, and its welfare exceeds that of $(17/18,1)$ by $1/40$ and that of $(0,1)$ by $9/20$. A second statement concerns the first display of the printed proofs. At the printed rule, the mean among the treated units is $1$ and the expected reward is $3/4$. Eight supporting statements give the steps, among them the formula $E[w]=(9u+10v)(4-u-v)/40$, the equality of $w_{\mathrm{ATT}}$ and $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$ when $\hat\mu_0=0$, and the identity $V(\pi)=E[\pi(X)(Y(1)-Y(0))]$ for two types. The two regrets appear as differences from the largest welfare, and the mean among the treated units appears as the ratio $A/q$ of the finding.

text.body: The corrected average-reward statement separates the assumptions for the two rewards of P006-E001. Let $n\ge1$ and let the covariate domain be countable with measurable singletons. For an admissible measurable policy $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, put $q=E[\pi(X)]$, $A=E[s(X)\pi(X)]$ and $h_n(q)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-q)^k$. The ATO block assumes the independent-unit outcome and treatment design conditions and integrable potential outcomes, with no estimator condition, and takes $s=\mu_1$. It asserts that the empty and nonempty treatment probabilities are $(1-q)^n$ and $1-(1-q)^n$, that the expected reward is $h_n(q)A$, equivalently $[1-(1-q)^n]A/q$ for $q>0$ and $0$ for $q=0$, and that its mean given a nonempty treated group is $A/q$ when $q>0$. Best responses are exactly the maximizers of $h_n(q)A$. The ATT block gives the same reward and best-response formulas with $s=\tau$, under the additional hypotheses that every evaluated estimator is integrable and $E[\hat\mu_0(X_i)\mid\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi]=\mu_0(X_i)$. Both rewards are defined to be zero when nobody is treated. A second statement takes finitely many values of $x$, with probabilities $p_j>0$ and $s_1\ge\dots\ge s_K$. It asserts that the threshold policy of the corrected proposition attains the largest $A$ among the policies such that $E[\pi(X)]=q$, and that some threshold policy maximizes $h_n(q)A$. It also asserts that the printed rule maximizes $A/q$ when $s_1>0$ and that the policy that treats nobody does so otherwise, where $A/q$ is set to $0$ for $q=0$. A third statement is this last assertion alone, without the requirement that the $p_j$ sum to one, and a fourth is the identity $h_1(q)A=A$.
text.headline: Propositions 6 and 7, as corrected
text.location: Appendix B.3, Propositions 6 and 7, PDF pp. 15–16; Section 3, PDF pp. 4–5

text.body: The main Lean statement is the bound of Proposition 2 with the replacement proof of P006-E001. Let $\Pi$ be a set of policies that contains $\pi\equiv0$, and suppose that $E[\hat\mu_0(X_i)\mid\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi]=\mu_0(X_i)$ for all $\pi\in\Pi$ and all units $i$. The statement asserts that every $\pi\in\Pi$ satisfies $V(\pi)=E[\pi(X)\tau(X)]$ and $E[w_{\mathrm{ATT}}]=h_n(q)V(\pi)$ with $h_n(q)\ge1$, where $q=E[\pi(X)]$ and $h_n(q)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-q)^k$. The policy $\pi\equiv0$ has expected reward $0$ and welfare $0$. Every best response $\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATT}}}$ in $\Pi$ then satisfies $V(\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATT}}})\ge0$ and $R(\pi^{w_{\mathrm{ATT}}})\le\max_{\pi\in\Pi}V(\pi)$. Three supporting statements give the steps separately. The first is $h_n(q)\ge1$ for $0\le q\le1$. The second is the same bound for any objective $h\cdot V$ such that $h\ge1$ on $\Pi$ and some policy in $\Pi$ has welfare $0$. The third says that a supremum equals the value at a maximizer. The statement is broader than the printed proposition in allowing any $\Pi$ that contains $\pi\equiv0$. It is narrower in requiring the covariate to take countably many values, as for the corrected Propositions 6 and 7. It also makes explicit the existence of a welfare-maximizing policy in $\Pi$, which the paper assumes when it uses a maximum.
text.headline: Proposition 2 (ATT Regret), with its proof replaced
text.location: Section 3, PDF p. 5; Appendix B.4, restatement and proof, PDF pp. 17–18

text.body: The Lean statements formalize Examples A and B of P006-E002, in which $n=1$, the covariate $X_1$ is $0$ or $1$ with probability $1/2$ each, and a policy is a pair $(p_0,p_1)$ in the unit square. The main statement asserts that both estimators have mean $0=\mu_0(x)$ at each fixed $x$, and that $\hat\mu_0(X_1)=1$ in Example A and $\hat\mu_0(X_1)=-1$ in Example B. In Example A the expected reward $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]$ is maximized only at $(0,0)$, welfare is maximized at $(1,1)$, the regret of $(0,0)$ is $1/2$, and $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]\ne V(\pi)$ at $(1,1)$. In Example B the expected reward is maximized only at $(1,1)$, welfare is maximized at $(0,0)$ with maximum $0$, and the regret of $(1,1)$ is $1/2$. A second statement adds a constant $U_1$ to Example A, so that $E[|\mu_0(X_1)-\mu_0(X_1,U_1)|]=0$, and asserts that the regret $1/2$ exceeds $2\gamma_{\mathrm{marg}}=0$. Three supporting statements give the expected reward of one unit, the formulas $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]=\mp(p_0+p_1)/4$ and $V(\pi)=\pm(p_0+p_1)/4$ in Examples A and B, and the equality of $w_{\mathrm{ATT}}$ and $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$ for $n=1$. The expected reward is the exact sum over the covariate and the treatment, and the estimator is a function of the observed covariate and of its argument $x$. The two conditional statements of the printed proofs fail because of the values of $\hat\mu_0(X_1)$, and the Lean statements do not write them as conditional expectations.

text.body: The Lean statements formalize Example C of P006-E002. Agents $j$ and $k$ have one unit each, their covariates $X_j$ and $X_k$ are independent and uniform on $\{0,1\}$, as is the reference covariate, and the weights $g_j$ and $g_k$ equal $1$. The untreated outcomes are $0$, the treated outcomes are $1/4$ for agent $j$ and $1/8$ for agent $k$, and both agents are scored with $\hat\mu_0(x)=\mathbf{1}\{x=X_j\}-\mathbf{1}\{x=X_k\}$. The main statement asserts that this estimator has mean $0$ at each fixed $x$, mean $1/2$ at $X_j$ given $X_j$, and mean $-1/2$ at $X_k$ given $X_k$. It asserts that the expected score of agent $j$ is maximized by treating nobody and that of agent $k$ by treating everyone, with maxima $0$ and $5/8$. A supporting statement gives the two expected scores, $-(p_{j,0}+p_{j,1})/8$ and $5(p_{k,0}+p_{k,1})/16$, as exact sums over both covariates and the treatment. The treatment effects are the constants $1/4$ and $1/8$. The premises of Definitions 1 and 2 then both reduce to $1/8\le1/4$, and they enter the statement in this form. The three covariate distributions coincide, so the example does not involve the direction of absolute continuity corrected in P006-E005.
text.headline: A counterexample to Theorem 2 (Ranking Desiderata Satisfied) under Assumption 1 as printed
text.location: Theorem 2, PDF p. 6; restatement and proof in Appendix C.2, PDF p. 20

text.body: Six Lean statements cover the corrected assumption of P006-E002 and its consequences for $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$. The assumption is written as $E[T_i^\pi(\hat\mu_0(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i))\mid X_i]=0$ for every feasible $\pi$ and every unit $i$, a form that needs no conditional mean where $\pi(X_i)=0$. Under it, the main statement asserts that $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]=nE[\pi(X)\tau(X)]=nV(\pi)$ for every $\pi$ in an arbitrary feasible set $\Pi$, where the expectation is taken over the estimator as well. A policy then maximizes the expected reward over $\Pi$ exactly when it maximizes $V$ over $\Pi$, and every best response has regret $0$. When $\Pi$ contains all policies, $\mathbf{1}(\tau(x)>0)$ is a best response. A second statement asserts that the assumption holds if $\hat\mu_0$ is unbiased at each fixed $x$ and is a measurable function of $x$ and of an auxiliary variable that is independent of $(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi)$. The other four statements take a covariate with finitely many values and an estimator whose distribution may depend on that value, so that expectations are finite sums. Two of them write the expected reward as $n$ times that of one unit. They assert the identity $E[w^g_{\mathrm{TT}}]=nE[g(X)\pi(X)\tau(X)]$ under the corrected assumption and, for $g\equiv1$, the conclusions of the main statement on maximizers and regret. The other two take one estimator that is drawn independently of the sample and applied to all $n$ units. They assert that the expected reward of the whole sample is $n$ times that of one unit, and that the identity holds when this estimator is unbiased at each fixed $x$. One statement of each pair is an algebraic identity, which holds without the constraints that make the weights probabilities.
text.headline: Assumption 1, as corrected, with Proposition 9 (TT Best Response) and Proposition 3 (TT Regret) under it
text.location: Assumption 1, PDF p. 4; Proposition 3, PDF p. 5; Proposition 9 and proof, PDF p. 17; Proposition 3 and proof, PDF p. 18

text.body: The main Lean statement is Theorem 1 with Assumption 1 replaced by the corrected assumption of P006-E002 and with $g(x)>0$ for all $x$. Let $\Pi$ be the set of all measurable $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$. The statement asserts that $E[w^g_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=nE[g(X_i)\tau(X_i)\pi(X_i)]$ for all $\pi\in\Pi$, and that $\pi^*(x)=\mathbf{1}(\tau(x)>0)$ maximizes this expected reward. It asserts further that every maximizer $\pi'$ satisfies $\pi'(X_i)=1$ almost surely on $\{\tau(X_i)>0\}$ and $\pi'(X_i)=0$ almost surely on $\{\tau(X_i)<0\}$. Every best response then has welfare $E[\tau(X_i)\mathbf{1}(\tau(X_i)>0)]$ and regret $0$. A second statement takes a covariate with finitely many values and asserts that, for $g>0$, the rule $\pi^*$ maximizes both $E[g(X)\tau(X)\pi(X)]$ and $E[\tau(X)\pi(X)]$ over all policies. A supporting statement is the inequality $\pi\tau\le\tau\,\mathbf{1}(\tau>0)$ for $0\le\pi\le1$. The weight $g$ is a fixed measurable function. The main statement assumes that $g\tau$, each term of the reward, and each unweighted treated estimator residual are integrable; it does not require integrability of the estimator at untreated evaluations. The weighted integrability conditions are substantive: finiteness of the expected total reward alone does not suffice for the corrected theorem. The second statement does not contain the identity for the expected reward, and it does not require the probabilities of the values to sum to one.
text.headline: Theorem 1 (Incentive Alignment), under the corrected Assumption 1 and with a strictly positive weight
text.location: Section 4, PDF p. 6; Appendix C.2, restatement and proof, PDF p. 19

text.body: The main Lean statement is Theorem 3 under the corrected assumption of P006-E002, which reads $E[T_i^\pi(\hat\mu_0(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i))\mid X_i,U_i]=0$ for every $\pi$ in an arbitrary feasible set $\Pi$. With $\widehat V(\pi)=E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]/n$, it asserts that, for all $\pi\in\Pi$, $\widehat V(\pi)=E\bigl[\pi(X_i,U_i)\bigl(\mu_1(X_i,U_i)-\mu_0(X_i)\bigr)\bigr],\qquad |\widehat V(\pi)-V(\pi)|\le E\bigl[|\mu_0(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i,U_i)|\bigr].$ It concludes that $R(\pi^{w_{\mathrm{TT}}})\le2\gamma$ for every best response, where $\gamma$ is any constant that satisfies Assumption 2. A second statement contains Lemma 2 and Proposition 10, with $\hat\mu_0$ kept inside the expectations. It asserts that $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]=n\bigl(E[\pi(X_i,U_i)\mu_1(X_i,U_i)]-E[\pi(X_i,U_i)\hat\mu_0(X_i)]\bigr)$ and that $R(\pi^w)\le2E[|\hat\mu_0(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i,U_i)|]$. A supporting statement gives the step common to both bounds: if $|\widehat V(\pi)-V(\pi)|\le\gamma$ for all $\pi\in\Pi$, then a maximizer of $\widehat V$ has regret at most $2\gamma$. The agent’s covariate is the pair $(X_i,U_i)$, the estimator does not depend on $U_i$, and $\mu_0(X_i)$ is the conditional mean of $\mu_0(X_i,U_i)$ given $X_i$. Both statements assume that a welfare-maximizing policy in $\Pi$ exists. The second statement is narrower than the printed lemma and proposition, since it has two further hypotheses. Given $(X_i,U_i)$, the mean of $T_i^\pi\hat\mu_0(X_i)$ is $\pi(X_i,U_i)$ times the mean of $\hat\mu_0(X_i)$, and the joint distribution of $(X_i,U_i,\hat\mu_0(X_i))$ depends neither on $\pi$ nor on $i$. An estimator from independent auxiliary data satisfies both.
text.headline: Theorem 3 (Regret With Information Asymmetry), under the corrected Assumption 1, with Lemma 2 and Proposition 10
text.location: Section 5, PDF p. 7; Appendix D.2, Lemma 2, Proposition 10 and Theorem 3, PDF pp. 21–22

text.body: Three Lean statements contain the arithmetic of P006-E009. Let $\hat\tau_1,\dots,\hat\tau_n$ be fitted effects of which $k\ge1$ are positive, let $S$ be the sum of the positive ones, and let $V=S/n$ and $b=S/k$. The first statement asserts that $b=V\cdot n/k$ and that $V<b$ when $k<n$. The second takes $b=V\cdot255/62$ with $0.1469535\le V\le0.1469545$ for the Horse Colic data, and $b=V\cdot7264/1360$ with $0.0251855\le V\le0.0251865$ for the Stroke data. It asserts that $b$ lies between $14989257/24800000$ and $14989359/24800000$ (about $0.6044$) in the first case and between $672601/5000000$ and $11434671/85000000$ (about $0.1345$) in the second. In particular $b>0.1475$ and $b>0.0255$. The third statement uses only the entries of Table 1. It asserts that $b>0.604$ if the utility is at least $0.14694$ and the treatment rate is positive and at most $0.2432$, and that $b>0.134$ if the utility is at least $0.02517$ and the rate is positive and at most $0.1873$. The counts and the bounds on $V$ are hypotheses of the second statement. The bounds come from six-decimal utilities stored in the released notebooks, which the paper does not print. The statements are exact arithmetic on these summaries, and they do not involve the data or the fit. The corrected wording of the two sentences has no formal statement.
text.headline: The two sentences of Section 6 on the average benefit among the units that would benefit, as corrected
text.location: Section 6, paragraphs “Horse Colic dataset” and “International Stroke Trial dataset”, PDF pp. 7–8; Table 1, PDF p. 9

text.body: The Lean statements formalize the example of P006-E003. In it $n=1$, the covariate takes a single value, $\Pi$ consists of the single policy that always treats, $w=w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$, and for $B>0$ the distribution has $Y(1)=1$ and $Y(0)=1+B$. The main statement asserts that the only feasible policy is a best response with $E[\pi(X)]=1$, so that Assumption 3 holds, that its welfare is $-B$, and that its regret is $0$. It asserts further that this policy has regret $0$ for every welfare function on $\Pi$. The policy that treats nobody is not in $\Pi$, and the bound $0\ge B$ of the printed proof is false. Four supporting statements concern the reward of one unit. They assert that $E[w_{\mathrm{ATO}}]=E[\pi(X)Y(1)]$ for every distribution and every policy, and that two distributions with the same joint distribution of $(X,Y(1))$ give the same expected reward for every measurable policy. This is the invariance hypothesis of the theorem for all pairs of distributions, and not only for the family indexed by $B$. A distribution is a probability measure on triples $(X,Y(0),Y(1))$, and the expected reward is the integral of the reward after the treatment of the unit is drawn with probability $\pi(X)$.
text.headline: A counterexample to Theorem 4, as printed
text.location: Appendix A.2, Assumption 3, Theorem 4 and its proof, PDF p. 14

text.body: The main Lean statement is the corrected theorem of P006-E003. Let $\Pi$ contain the policy $\pi\equiv0$, and let $w$ satisfy Assumption 3. Suppose that, for all $\pi\in\Pi$, the expected reward is the same under any two distributions with finite means and the same joint distribution of $(X,Y(1))$. The statement asserts that for every $M>0$ there exist a distribution $\mathcal D$ with finite means and a best response $\pi_*$ under $\mathcal D$ such that $R_{\mathcal D}(\pi_*)>M$. It also contains the construction. Let $\pi_*$ be a best response under a distribution $\mathcal D_*$ such that $c=E_{\mathcal D_*}[\pi_*(X)]>0$, and for $B>0$ let $\mathcal D_B$ keep the joint distribution of $(X,Y(1))$ and set $Y(0)=Y(1)+B$. Then $\pi_*$ is a best response under $\mathcal D_B$, every $\pi\in\Pi$ has welfare $-B\,E[\pi(X)]$, the largest welfare is $0$, and $R_{\mathcal D_B}(\pi_*)=Bc$. A second statement is the arithmetic $Bc>M$ for $B=(M+1)/c$. The expected reward enters as an arbitrary function of the policy and of the distribution of $(X,Y(0),Y(1))$ for one unit. The statement then applies to every reward and every sample size for which the invariance holds. Welfare is $E[\pi(X)(Y(1)-Y(0))]$, the form given by Lemma 1. The example with $w\equiv0$ in P006-E003, which shows that the conclusion cannot hold for every best response, has no formal statement.
text.headline: Theorem 4, as corrected
text.location: Appendix A.2, PDF p. 14

text.body: The Lean statements formalize the example of P006-E005, in which $P_{X^k}$ is Lebesgue measure $L$ on $[0,1]$ and $P_{X_0}=(L+\delta_{1/2})/2$. The main statement asserts that both are probability measures with support $[0,1]$, and that $P_{X^k}$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $P_{X_0}$, which is the printed condition. It asserts further that $P_{X^k}(\{1/2\})=0$ and $P_{X_0}(\{1/2\})=1/2$, and that $P_{X_0}$ is not absolutely continuous with respect to $P_{X^k}$. It concludes that no nonnegative measurable $f$ satisfies $P_{X_0}(C)=\int_Cf\,dP_{X^k}$ for all Borel sets $C$. A supporting statement says that multiplying a measure by a nonzero constant does not change its support. Both measures are defined on the real line and vanish outside $[0,1]$, which changes neither the null sets nor the supports. The statements concern the existence of the derivative $dP_{X_0}/dP_{X^k}$ and not the ranking conclusion. The rest of the model, two agents with one unit each and equal treatment effects, is not part of them.
text.headline: A counterexample to the condition of absolute continuity in the first sentence of Theorem 2, as printed
text.location: Theorem 2, PDF p. 6; restatement in Appendix C.2, PDF p. 20

text.body: The corrected ranking statement uses each agent’s own sample and unit covariates, with $P_0\ll P_{X^{(k)}}$ and normalized weight $g_k=n_k^{-1}dP_0/dP_{X^{(k)}}$. It assumes the independent-unit outcome and treatment design conditions, $E_{P_0}|\tau^{(k)}|<\infty$, and ordinary integrable treated estimator residuals $T_i^{\pi_k}\{\hat\mu_0(X_i^{(k)})-\mu_0(X_i^{(k)})\}$ with conditional mean zero given the unit covariate, for every agent, admissible policy and unit. Each individual weighted reward summand $(Y_i^{(k)}-\hat\mu_0(X_i^{(k)}))T_i^{\pi_k}g_k(X_i^{(k)})$ is also assumed absolutely integrable. Integrability at untreated estimator evaluations is not required. Agents may have different measurable sample spaces, and the covariate domain is an arbitrary measurable space, without a support-equality condition. The weight may vanish, and mutual absolute continuity is not assumed. For every admissible policy, $E[w_k]=n_k\int\tau^{(k)}\pi_k g_k\,dP_{X^{(k)}}=\int\tau^{(k)}\pi_k\,dP_0.$ The policy $\mathbf1\{\tau^{(k)}>0\}$ attains the maximum $\int\max(\tau^{(k)},0)\,dP_0$. Pointwise dominance implies dominance of these maxima without a sign restriction. If all effects are nonnegative, each maximum equals $\int\tau^{(k)}\,dP_0$ and reference-mean dominance gives the same ordering of the maxima. The common untreated conditional mean is retained; a common full untreated conditional distribution, as in Appendix C.1, is stronger than this premise.
text.headline: Theorem 2 (Ranking Desiderata Satisfied), as corrected
text.location: Theorem 2, PDF p. 6; restatement, equation (2) and proof in Appendix C.2, PDF p. 20

text.body: Most of P006-E013 corrects indices and the order of arguments, and these corrections enter the formal definitions and not a statement. In the definitions each agent’s score takes that agent’s own covariates, treatments and outcomes, in the order $(\mathbf X,\mathbf T,\mathbf Y)$. The weight of Reward Function 4 is evaluated at the covariate of each unit, as in the corrected equation (2). Definitions 1 and 2 compare the largest expected score of agent $j$ on its own sample with that of agent $k$ on its own sample. The Lean statement is the inequality from which the corrected proof of Theorem 2 obtains Definition 1: if $\tau^{(j)}(x)\ge\tau^{(k)}(x)$ for all $x\in\mathcal X$, then $E[\tau^{(j)}(X_0)\,\mathbf{1}(\tau^{(j)}(X_0)>0)]\ge E[\tau^{(k)}(X_0)\,\mathbf{1}(\tau^{(k)}(X_0)>0)].$ A supporting statement is the identity $t\,\mathbf{1}(t>0)=\max(t,0)$. The statement assumes that both expectations are finite. It does not require $P_{X_0}$ to be a probability measure, and it is broader than the correction in this respect. In the two definitions a supremum stands for the maximum over the feasible set, and the two agree whenever the maximum is attained. The identities for the expected scores in the proofs of Proposition 4 and of Theorems 1 and 2 belong to the Lean statements for those results.
text.headline: Definitions 1 and 2, equation (2) and the score displays of Appendix C, with each agent’s own arguments and indices
text.location: Definitions 1 and 2, PDF p. 5; proofs of Proposition 4 and Theorem 1, PDF p. 19; equation (2) and proof of Theorem 2, PDF p. 20

text.body: The Lean statements formalize the two examples of P006-E006. In the first, $X$ and $U$ are constant, the only policy treats with probability $1$, and $Y(1)=1$. The main statement asserts that the observed pair $(T,Y)$ has the same distribution for $Y(0)=0$ and for $Y(0)=2$, while the probability of treatment is positive and the probability of an untreated unit is $0$. In the second, $X$ is $0$ or $1$ with probability $1/2$ each, $\pi(0)=1$, $\pi(1)=1/2$ and $Y(1)=1$. Either $Y(0)=0$ at both values of $X$, or $Y(0)=2$ at $X=0$ and $Y(0)=0$ at $X=1$. The statement asserts that $(X,T,Y)$ has the same distribution in both cases, with probabilities $1/2$, $1/4$ and $1/4$ for $(0,1,1)$, $(1,1,1)$ and $(1,0,0)$. Both treatment probabilities are positive, $P(T^\pi=0)=1/4$, and $P(T^\pi=0\mid X=0)=0$. A second statement asserts that $\Delta(x,u)=0$ when $U$ takes a single value, so that Assumption 4 holds with $\gamma_{\max}=0$ in every case. Potential outcomes are functions of the covariate, and the distribution of the observed data is an exact sum over the covariate and the treatment. The statements concern the identification of $\mu_0$ and the hypothesis of Lemma 3. They contain no instance in which $\hat\mu_0^\pi$ is defined and the bound $2\gamma_{\max}$ fails.
text.headline: Counterexamples to the positivity condition of Appendix D.3 and Theorem 5, as printed
text.location: Appendix D.3, first paragraph and Theorem 5, PDF p. 23; proof of Theorem 5 and Lemma 3, PDF p. 24

text.body: The main Lean statement is the corrected Theorem 5 of P006-E006. Let $q_\pi(x)=P(T^\pi=0\mid X=x)=E[1-\pi(x,U)\mid X=x]$, and suppose that, for every $\pi$ in an arbitrary feasible set $\Pi$, $q_\pi(x)>0$ for almost every $x$. The estimate is $\hat\mu_0^\pi(x)=E[\mu_0(x,U)(1-\pi(x,U))\mid X=x]/q_\pi(x)$. For almost every $x$, as in Lemma 3, the statement asserts that the density $(1-\pi(x,u))/q_\pi(x)$ defines a probability distribution of $U$ given $X=x$ and $T^\pi=0$. It asserts that $\hat\mu_0^\pi(x)$ is the mean of $\mu_0(x,\cdot)$ under this distribution, and that $\hat\mu_0^\pi(x)$ lies between the smallest and the largest value of $\mu_0(x,u)$. It asserts further that $|\hat\mu_0^\pi(x)-\mu_0(x,u)|\le\Delta(x,u)$ for almost every $x$ and every $u$, and that $\tfrac1nE[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]=E\bigl[\pi(X,U)\bigl(\mu_1(X,U)-\hat\mu_0^\pi(X)\bigr)\bigr],\qquad \bigl|\tfrac1nE[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]-V(\pi)\bigr|\le E[\Delta(X,U)].$ It concludes that $R(\pi^w)\le2\gamma$ for every best response, where $\gamma$ is any constant that satisfies Assumption 4. A second statement asserts that $\pi(x,u)<1$ for all $x$ and $u$ implies $q_\pi(x)>0$ for all $x$. It also asserts that $\hat\mu_0^\pi(x)=\mu_0(x)$ when $\mu_0(x,u)$ does not depend on $u$. This clause allows the policy to depend on $u$; the corrected first paragraph instead takes the policy to depend on $x$ only. A supporting statement says that a weighted mean of finitely many numbers lies between any lower and any upper bound for them. The distribution of $U$ given $X$ is a Markov kernel, and $\hat\mu_0^\pi$ is a population quantity and not an estimate from a finite sample. The main statement assumes that the minima and maxima over $u$ in Lemma 3 and in $\Delta(x,u)$ are attained, that $\Delta$ is integrable, and that a welfare-maximizing policy in $\Pi$ exists.
text.headline: Theorem 5 and the first paragraph of Appendix D.3, as corrected, with Lemma 3
text.location: Appendix D.3, first paragraph, Assumption 4 and Theorem 5, PDF p. 23; proof of Theorem 5 and Lemma 3, PDF p. 24

text.body: Three Lean statements cover the computation of P006-E014 and the companion claim of the same paragraph. Fix $x$, and let $U$ given $X=x$ take finitely many values $u$ with probabilities $p_u>0$, so that $\hat\mu_0^\pi(x)=\frac{\sum_u\mu_0(x,u)\,p_u(1-\pi(x,u))}{\sum_up_u(1-\pi(x,u))}.$ The main statement asserts that, when only the type $\tilde u$ is left untreated, an untreated unit has probability $p_{\tilde u}$ and $\hat\mu_0^\pi(x)=\mu_0(x,\tilde u)$. When only the type $\tilde u$ is treated and there exists another type, $\hat\mu_0^\pi(x)$ is the weighted mean of $\mu_0(x,u)$ over $u\ne\tilde u$. The second statement is the example of three equally likely types with $\mu_0(x,u)$ equal to $0$, $1$ and $3$. There the estimate is $2$ when only the first type is treated and $0$ when only the first type is left untreated. The third negates the unrestricted assertion that $E[|\mu_0(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i,U_i)|]\le E[\Delta(X,U)]$ on general measurable spaces under the standing experiment assumptions and the marginal baseline condition, even assuming that the maxima in $\Delta(x,u)$ are attained and that $\Delta$ is integrable. The comparison holds, under the stated integrability conditions, when $U$ has a conditional distribution $K(x,dv)$ given $X$: then $\mu_0(x)=\int\mu_0(x,v)K(x,dv)$ and $\Delta(x,u)=\max_v|\mu_0(x,u)-\mu_0(x,v)|$ bounds $|\mu_0(x)-\mu_0(x,u)|$ almost surely (see P006-N011); on that domain, Assumption 4 with the constant $\gamma_{\max}$ implies Assumption 2 with $\gamma_{\mathrm{marg}}=\gamma_{\max}$. The first two statements are for finitely many types of positive probability, since a single value of a continuous $U$ cannot be left untreated with positive probability. The claim that Assumption 2 is not sufficient to bound the regret is the paper’s own, and no Lean statement asserts it.
text.headline: The sentence beginning “Intuitively” in Appendix D.3, as corrected
text.location: Appendix D.3, paragraph after Assumption 4, PDF p. 23

text.body: The Lean statement formalizes the example of P006-E007 with $p=1/2$, $\alpha=-1$, $\beta=4$ and $n=2$, so that $\mu_1=(0,1)$, $\mu_0=(-1,4)$ and $\tau=(1,-3)$. A policy is a pair $(\pi(0),\pi(1))$ in the unit square. The statement asserts that $(0,1)$ maximizes the expected reward under $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$ over all such pairs, with expected reward $3/4$, and that $(1,0)$ maximizes welfare. It asserts that the regret of $(0,1)$ is $2$, while the printed expression $1-p\beta$ equals $-1$. The expected reward is the exact sum over the 16 combinations of types and treatments of the two units, and the reward is $0$ when nobody is treated. The best response is thus obtained from the reward as defined, and not from the rule of Proposition 6, which P006-E001 corrects. The statement asserts that $(0,1)$ is a maximizer of the expected reward, and not that it is the only one.
text.headline: A counterexample to the regret display for the second failure mode in the proof of Proposition 1, as printed
text.location: Appendix B.4, proof of Proposition 1, second failure mode, PDF p. 17

text.body: Two Lean statements cover the corrected display of P006-E007. In the family of the proof, with $0<p<1$, $\alpha=-1$ and $\beta>1$, the treatment effects are $\tau(0)=1$ and $\tau(1)=1-\beta$, and welfare is $V(\pi)=(1-p)\pi(0)+p(1-\beta)\pi(1)$. The first statement asserts that welfare is maximized over all policies by treating $x=0$ only, with maximum $1-p$, and that the policy $\pi^w$ with $\pi^w(0)=0$ and $\pi^w(1)=1$ has welfare $p(1-\beta)$. It asserts that $R(\pi^w)=1-2p+p\beta ,$ which exceeds the printed value $1-p\beta$ by $2p(\beta-1)>0$. The second statement asserts that $1-2p+p\beta\to\infty$ as $\beta\to\infty$, for every $p>0$. Both statements concern the welfare of the fixed policy $\pi^w$. They do not assert that $\pi^w$ is a best response to $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$; a separate statement asserts that $\pi^w$ maximizes the expected reward for $n=2$. The second statement is broader than the proof needs, since it does not require $p<1$.
text.headline: The regret display for the second failure mode in the proof of Proposition 1, as corrected
text.location: Appendix B.4, proof of Proposition 1, second failure mode, PDF p. 17

text.body: The Lean statement formalizes the example of P006-E008, in which $X$ is constant and $(Y(0),Y(1))$ equals $(1,1)$, $(1,-1)$, $(-1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$ with probabilities $1/8$, $3/8$, $1/8$ and $3/8$. It asserts that these probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one, that $P(Y(0)=1)=1/2=\sigma(0)$ and $P(Y(1)=1)=1/4=\sigma(-\log3)$, and that $E[Y(0)]=0$ and $E[Y(1)]=-1/2$. The distribution then belongs to the printed logistic model with $\beta_0=0$, $\beta_2=-\log3$ and $\beta_1=\beta_3=0$, while the printed formula gives $\mu_1=1/4$ where the mean is $-1/2$. The statement also asserts that the rule $\mu_1(x)>0$ treats nobody at the mean $-1/2$ and everybody at the value $\sigma(-\log3)$. Each potential outcome is represented by the indicator that the horse lives, with the coded value $1$ or $-1$. The two coefficients enter only through the values $\sigma(0)$ and $\sigma(-\log3)$. The rule $\mu_1(x)>0$ is the paper’s response to the reward $w_{\mathrm{TO}}$, and the statement does not compute a regret.
text.headline: A counterexample to the formula for $\mu_t(x)$ in Appendix E.2.1, as printed
text.location: Appendix E.2.1, paragraph beginning “We trained a logistic regression model”, PDF p. 25

text.body: The main Lean statement is the corrected formula of P006-E008. For coefficients $\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_2,\hat\beta_3$ and a covariate vector $x$, let $\eta_t(x)=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1^\top x+\hat\beta_2t+\hat\beta_3^\top xt$. The statement asserts that an outcome equal to $1$ with probability $\sigma(\eta_t(x))$ and to $-1$ otherwise has mean $2\sigma(\eta_t(x))-1$, for $t=0$ and for $t=1$. It asserts that the difference of the two means is $2(\sigma(\eta_1(x))-\sigma(\eta_0(x)))$, and that $2\sigma(z)-1\ne\sigma(z)$ for all real $z$. Two supporting statements are the bounds $0<\sigma(z)<1$ and the mean $2p-1$ of an outcome that equals $1$ with probability $p$ and $-1$ otherwise. The covariate vector has an arbitrary finite dimension, and each mean is the sum of the two values weighted by their probabilities. The statement holds for all values of the coefficients, and it makes no assertion about the fit to the Horse Colic data.
text.headline: The formula for $\mu_t(x)$ in Appendix E.2.1, as corrected
text.location: Appendix E.2.1, paragraph beginning “We trained a logistic regression model”, PDF p. 25

text.body: Two Lean statements cover the corrected formula of P006-E015. For observations $i=1,\dots,n$ with feature values $X_i$ and numbers $m_i=\mu_0(X_i,U_i)$, the corrected $\mu_0(x)$ is the sum of $m_i$ over the observations with $X_i=x$, divided by the number of these observations. The first statement asserts, for every $x$ that occurs in the sample, that $\mu_0(x)$ lies between any lower and any upper bound for these $m_i$, and that $\sum_{i:X_i=x}(m_i-\mu_0(x))=0$. It also asserts that $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mu_0(X_i)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nm_i .$ The second statement is the example of two observations with the same feature value and $m=(1,3)$. There the corrected mean is $2$, and the group sum divided by $1$ is $4$. The feature values may lie in any set, and $n\ge1$. The bounds are stated for arbitrary lower and upper bounds, which include the minimum and the maximum of the group. The printed quotient has a free index in its denominator and is not a formal object, and the second statement represents it by the group sum.
text.headline: The empirical conditional mean $\mu_0(x)$ of Appendix E.4, as corrected
text.location: Appendix E.4, first displayed formula, PDF p. 26

text.body: The Lean statement formalizes the two distributions of P006-N005, with a single value of $X$, $Y(1)=1$, and treatment assigned with probability $1/2$ independently of $Y(0)$. Each distribution is the table of the probabilities of $(Y(0),T,R)$, where $R=1$ when the outcome is observed, and treated outcomes are always observed. The statement asserts that both tables are probability distributions in which $T$ is independent of $Y(0)$. In both, an untreated unit has probability $1/2$, and an untreated unit with an observed outcome has probability $1/4$. It asserts that every possible observation $(T,R,Z)$, where $Z$ is missing when $R=0$, has the same probability under the two distributions. It asserts further that $\mu_0$ equals $1/2$ under the first distribution and $3/4$ under the second, while the mean of the observed untreated outcomes is $3/4$ under both. Since $X$ and $Y(1)$ are constant, the tables leave them out. The indicator $R$ is not a symbol of the paper, and it formalizes the phrase “observed a fraction of outcomes for untreated units”.
text.headline: A counterexample to the sufficient conditions of Appendix A.1, item 2, as printed
text.location: Appendix A.1, item 2 (“Untreated patients in the treatment population”), conditions (a) and (b), PDF p. 13

text.body: Four Lean statements cover the corrected conditions of P006-N005. They are stated at one value $x$ of the covariate, for the distribution of $(Y_i(0),Y_i(1),T_i^\pi,R_i)$ given $X_i=x$, where $R_i=1$ when $Y_i$ is observed. The hypotheses are that the potential outcomes are independent of $T_i^\pi$, that $P(T_i^\pi=0)>0$, and that $P(T_i^\pi=0,R_i=1)>0$. The main statement has three parts. If $E[Y_i(0)\mid T_i^\pi=0,R_i=1]=E[Y_i(0)\mid T_i^\pi=0]$, then $\mu_0(x)=E[Y_i\mid T_i^\pi=0,R_i=1]$. If $q=P(R_i=1\mid T_i^\pi=0)<1$, then $\mu_0(x)=qm_1+(1-q)m_0$, where $m_1$ and $m_0$ are the means of $Y_i(0)$ among the untreated units with observed and with missing outcomes, and $m_1=\mu_0(x)$ if and only if $m_1=m_0$. If $Y_i(0)$ is independent of $R_i$ among the untreated units, then the first condition holds. Two further statements are the first part alone and the equivalence $m_1=qm_1+(1-q)m_0\iff m_1=m_0$ for $0<q<1$. A supporting statement says that $E[Y_i(0)\mid T_i^\pi=0]=E[Y_i(0)]$ when $Y_i(0)$ is independent of $T_i^\pi$. A conditional mean is the integral over an event divided by the probability of the event. The statements hold for every distribution at a fixed $x$. They do not derive the distribution given $X_i=x$ from a joint distribution with $X_i$, and they are narrower than the correction in this respect.
text.headline: The sufficient conditions of Appendix A.1, item 2, as corrected
text.location: Appendix A.1, item 2 (“Untreated patients in the treatment population”), PDF p. 13

text.body: The Lean statements cover Proposition 5 and the construction of its proof, in which the display reads $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]=nE[\pi(X_i,U_i)(\mu_1(X_i,U_i)-\mu_0(X_i))]$ as corrected in P006-N006. Here $X$ is constant, $U$ is $0$ or $1$ with probability $1/2$ each, $\hat\mu_0=\mu_0(x)=0$, and a policy is the pair $(p_0,p_1)$ of its treatment probabilities at $u=0$ and $u=1$. The main statement asserts that for every $n\ge1$, $\alpha>0$ and $\epsilon>0$ there exists $\beta\in(0,\alpha)$ such that the printed policy $(1,0)$ is a best response and its regret is at least $\gamma_{\mathrm{marg}}-\epsilon$. A second statement describes the family for $0<\beta<\alpha$. The expected reward is $n\beta p_0/2$, the best responses are exactly the policies such that $p_0=1$, the largest welfare is $\alpha/2$ at $(0,1)$, a best response has regret $\alpha-\beta/2-\alpha p_1/2$, and $E[|\mu_0(X_i)-\mu_0(X_i,U_i)|]=\alpha$. A third replaces $\mu_1(x,1)=0$ by $-\eta$ and takes $\eta=\beta$. It asserts that, for some $\beta\in(0,\alpha)$, the policy $(1,0)$ is the only best response and its regret $\alpha-\beta$ is at least $\gamma_{\mathrm{marg}}-\epsilon$. A fourth asserts that the expected reward of $n$ independent units, summed over all their types and treatments, is $n$ times that of one unit. Seven supporting statements give the formulas for reward and welfare, the two sets of best responses, the largest welfare and the value $\gamma_{\mathrm{marg}}=\alpha$. Two of them are general: a positive factor does not change the maximizers, and the expectation of a sum over $n$ independent units is $n$ times that of one term. The proposition is read as the existence of a best response with the stated regret, as its proof reads it. The main statement takes $\beta<\alpha$, since the printed choice $\beta=\epsilon$ needs $\epsilon<\alpha$.
text.headline: Proposition 5, with the reward display of its proof as corrected
text.location: Section 5, PDF p. 7; Appendix D.2, restatement and proof, PDF pp. 22–23

text.body: The Lean statement negates the universal conjunction of the two propositions as printed. Let $X$ be discrete, let $\Pi$ be the set of all policies $\pi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, and let the estimator satisfy Assumption 1 in its printed form, $E[\hat\mu_0(x)]=\mu_0(x)$ for all $x$. The claim being disproved asserts that the rule $\mathbf{1}(x\in\arg\max_x\mu_1(x)\text{ and }\mu_1(x)>0)$ maximizes $E[w_{\mathrm{ATO}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]$ over $\Pi$. It asserts the same for $w_{\mathrm{ATT}}$, with $\tau$ in place of $\mu_1$. The expected reward is the expectation over the $n$ units, the treatment randomization and the estimator, and the reward is $0$ when nobody is treated. This is the claim that the counterexample with two units of P006-E001 contradicts, and the counterexample and the corrected propositions have their own Lean statements. A discrete $X$ is represented by a covariate with countably many values. The two propositions are joined in one statement, so that Assumption 1 is a hypothesis for $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$ as well, which Proposition 6 does not require. The sentences of Section 3 that restate the two rules in words have no separate statement.
text.headline: Propositions 6 and 7 (ATO and ATT Best Response), as printed
text.location: Appendix B.3, Propositions 6 and 7, PDF pp. 15–16; Section 3, PDF pp. 4–5

text.body: The Lean statement negates the universal claim of Propositions 9 and 3 with Assumption 1 as printed, $E[\hat\mu_0(x)]=\mu_0(x)$ for each fixed $x$, as the only condition on the estimator. For an arbitrary feasible set $\Pi$, the claim being disproved asserts that $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}(\mathbf X,\mathbf T^\pi,\mathbf Y)]=nV(\pi)$ for all $\pi\in\Pi$, which is the identity in the proof of Proposition 9. The claim asserts that a policy maximizes the expected reward over $\Pi$ exactly when it maximizes $V$ over $\Pi$, and that every best response has regret $0$. This is Proposition 3 with its remark that the regret is zero “regardless of the feasible set $\Pi$”. When $\Pi$ is the set of all policies, the claim asserts that $\mathbf{1}(\tau(x)>0)$ is a best response, as in Proposition 9. The estimator is a random function, and the expected reward integrates over it. This is the claim that Example A of P006-E002 contradicts, and the examples and the corrected statement have their own Lean statements. The inference from Assumption 1 in the printed proof is not a separate statement, and it enters through the identity $E[w_{\mathrm{TT}}]=nV(\pi)$.
text.headline: Proposition 9 (TT Best Response) and Proposition 3 (TT Regret) under Assumption 1, as printed
text.location: Assumption 1, PDF p. 4; Proposition 3, PDF p. 5; Proposition 9 and proof, PDF p. 17; Proposition 3 and proof, PDF p. 18

text.body: The Lean statement negates the universal conditional reporting claim obtained from the two sentences. Let $b$ be the average of the fitted effects over the units whose fitted effect is positive. The sentences are read as saying that $b$ equals $0.147$ for the horses and $0.025$ for the patients, to three decimals, that is, $0.1465\le b<0.1475$ and $0.0245\le b<0.0255$. The hypotheses are those of the corrected statement, with $V$ the utility under $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$. For the Horse Colic data, $b=V\cdot255/62$ with $0.1469535\le V\le0.1469545$. For the Stroke data, $b=V\cdot7264/1360$ with $0.0251855\le V\le0.0251865$. The statement negates the assertion that every real tuple satisfying these hypotheses satisfies both reporting intervals. These hypotheses can be satisfied. The stronger implication that every such tuple has $b>0.1475$ for the horses and $b>0.0255$ for the patients is stated separately under P006-T9, in the numerical-interval statement for P006-E009. The six-decimal utility bounds and the Horse Colic analysis-sample size $255$ are supplied source summaries. The paper prints the beneficiary counts $62$ and $1360$ and the Stroke analysis-sample size $7264$. The statement tests the two sentences against these summaries, and it does not involve the data or the fit.
text.headline: The two sentences of Section 6 on the average benefit among the units that would benefit, as printed
text.location: Section 6, paragraphs “Horse Colic dataset” and “International Stroke Trial dataset”, PDF pp. 7–8

text.body: The words “may be arbitrarily large” are read as follows: for every $M>0$ there exist a distribution and a best response to $w_{\mathrm{ATO}}$, over the set of all policies, such that the regret of this best response exceeds $M$. The main Lean statement asserts this in the family of the printed proof, with $n=2$, $p=1/2$, $\mu_1=(0,1)$ and $\mu_0=(\alpha,0)$. There exists $\alpha<0$ such that the policy $(\pi(0),\pi(1))=(0,1)$ maximizes the expected reward, the policy that treats everyone maximizes welfare, and the regret of $(0,1)$ exceeds $M$. Three further statements concern the family for every $n\ge1$ and $0<p<1$. The first asserts that the expected reward is $h_n(q)\,p\,\pi(1)$, where $q=(1-p)\pi(0)+p\pi(1)$ and $h_n(q)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-q)^k$. It asserts that $(0,1)$ is the only best response for $n\ge2$, and that for $n=1$ the best responses are the policies such that $\pi(1)=1$. It also contains the first failure mode: for $\alpha<0$ and $\beta=0$ the largest welfare is $-\alpha(1-p)+p$, and the regret of $(0,1)$ is $-\alpha(1-p)$. The second states these two formulas alone, and the third asserts that $-\alpha(1-p)\to\infty$ as $\alpha\to-\infty$, for every $p<1$. A supporting statement asserts that $(0,1)$ maximizes the expected reward for $n=2$ and $0<p<1$. The expected reward is the exact sum over the types and treatments of the units, and the best response is not taken from Proposition 6. The main statement uses one value of $n$ and one of $p$, which suffices for the reading above.
text.headline: Proposition 1 (ATO Regret)
text.location: Section 3, PDF p. 4; Appendix B.4, restatement and proof, PDF p. 17

text.body: The words “will be violated” are read as an existence statement. There exist two agents such that the premises of Definitions 1 and 2 hold and the ordering of their largest expected scores fails. The Lean statement describes such a pair. Agents $j$ and $k$ have covariates uniform on $\{0,1\}$, untreated outcomes $0$, treated outcomes $1$, the estimator $\hat\mu_0=0$, and sample sizes $n_j=1$ and $n_k=2$. Each agent is scored with $w_{\mathrm{TT}}$ on its own sample, as in the definitions corrected in P006-E013. The statement asserts that treating everyone maximizes the expected score of each agent over all policies, and that the two maxima are $1$ and $2$, so that agent $j$ has the smaller one. Since $\tau^{(j)}=\tau^{(k)}\equiv1$, the premises $\tau^{(j)}(x)\ge\tau^{(k)}(x)$ and $E[\tau^{(j)}(X_0)]\ge E[\tau^{(k)}(X_0)]$ both reduce to $1\le1$, and they enter the statement in this form. The expected scores are exact sums over the types and treatments of one unit and of two units. The statement covers this instance only. It does not contain the identity $\max_{\pi_k}E[w_k]=n_kE[\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})\,\mathbf{1}(\tau^{(k)}(X^{(k)})>0)]$ of the printed proof, nor the general choice of $n_j$ and $n_k$.
